los.description: Compute standard errors and intervals for an evaluation score that account for clustered items, repeated samples and small item counts, given item-level results where questions share source documents
Decide whether the difference between two systems is real and large enough to matter, using a paired analysis, given item-level results for two configurations and a minimum effect
Design an evaluation's size in items, samples per item and grader calls to detect a stated difference within budget, given pilot variances and unit costs
Evaluate the bias that grader error adds to a pass rate and correct it, carrying calibration uncertainty into the interval, given a model grader with 300 human-labelled verdicts in two languages
Audit an evaluation claim for statistical validity, contamination risk and unequal tuning or token budgets, given a leaderboard-style report on four systems
Design a reporting standard for evaluation claims, including results by language and subgroup, given the audit findings and a release process

questions.prompt: Configuration B scores 69.8% on the 600 questions, 95% interval 66.7% to 72.9%. A manager asks what the interval means. Which answer is right?
options: B passes between 66.7% and 72.9% of these 600 questions
B's pass rate on questions written the same way is plausibly between 66.7% and 72.9%
Each answer of B passes with a probability between 66.7% and 72.9%
B will score between 66.7% and 72.9% on next year's regulations
questions.explanation: The interval estimates the pass rate on the population the questions were sampled from; on the sample itself there is no uncertainty, and other populations are not covered.
misconceptions: Treats the 600 questions as the population: on them the rate is known exactly
Reads the interval as a range of individual answers, not of a rate
Assumes the interval covers any population, including questions of a different kind

questions.prompt: C's design effect is 2.5. Furat can pay for 160 more questions. Which plan narrows C's clustered interval most?
options: 160 questions from the same 80 documents, two per document
Ten samples per question in place of five
160 questions from 20 new documents
Report the naive interval, which is already narrower
questions.explanation: The clustered standard error falls with the number of documents; new documents add independent evidence that more questions from old documents do not.
misconceptions: Treats questions as independent: more questions from the same documents carry the same document effects
Confuses sampling noise with clustering: more samples shrink the within-item part only
Believes the naive formula is the safer report: it is narrower because it is wrong

questions.prompt: At temperature 0.2, D's between-item variance is 0.123 and its within-item variance 0.068. A colleague proposes 20 samples per question in place of 5 to "make the score precise". What happens?
options: The standard error barely falls, because the between-item part does not shrink with samples
The standard error halves, as it would with four times the questions
The pass rate rises, because more samples find more right answers
The score becomes pass@20, which is the right metric at last
questions.explanation: More samples reduce only the within / K term; the between-item term, 0.123 here, stays, so the SE goes from 0.0151 to 0.0145.
misconceptions: Treats samples as independent questions: they share the question's difficulty
Confuses precision with bias: more samples change the noise, not the expected score
Mistakes pass@k for the mean: the mean is unchanged in expectation

questions.prompt: The plan named the mean pass rate. After the run, D beats C on pass@5 but not on the mean. The team wants to headline pass@5 "because it shows D's potential". What should the report do?
options: Headline pass@5, since it is a recognised metric
Headline pass@5 with alpha lowered to 0.01
Delete pass@5 from the report entirely
Headline the planned mean and label pass@5 as an unplanned, exploratory result
questions.explanation: The planned metric carries the stated error rate; an outcome chosen because it won does not, so it can be shown only as exploratory.
misconceptions: Treats any defensible metric as equal once results are known: that is the forking path
Believes a lower alpha repairs a post hoc choice: it does not undo the selection
Thinks a plan forbids any other result: secondary results are allowed when labelled

questions.prompt: A new task set has 400 questions from 40 documents. The naive standard error of a configuration's score is 0.020 and the clustered one is 0.032. Which should the report use, and what does it imply?
options: The naive one: it is more precise
The mean of the two, 0.026
Either, if each question was sampled five times
The clustered one: the 400 questions are worth about 156 independent ones
questions.explanation: Questions from one document share its difficulty; DEFF = (0.032 / 0.020)² = 2.56, so 400 / 2.56 ≈ 156.
misconceptions: Thinks the narrower interval is the more precise one, when it is narrower only because it ignores clustering
Averages two estimates as if both were valid
Believes repeated samples fix clustering, which comes from documents, not draws

questions.prompt: Two configurations answer the same 500 questions. Their scores' intervals overlap heavily. A colleague concludes there is no difference. What is wrong with that?
options: Overlapping separate intervals ignore the correlation; the paired interval of the difference can exclude zero
The intervals should have been clustered first
Nothing: overlapping intervals mean no difference
The difference must be checked against the minimum effect before anything else
questions.explanation: Shared questions make the scores correlated; the variance of their difference subtracts twice the covariance, so the paired interval is much narrower than the overlap suggests.
misconceptions: Thinks clustering is the missing piece, when it barely changes a paired difference
Believes overlap is always conclusive, which is true only for independent samples, and then only roughly
Confuses the size of the effect with the evidence for it

questions.prompt: Of six configurations, F has the highest pass rate. After Holm adjustment F is separated from A, B and C, but not from D or E. What may the release note say?
options: F is the best configuration
F is the best, because it beats D at the 25% level
F, D and E are tied at the top; F is better than A, B and C
F, D and E are shown to be equally good
questions.explanation: The adjusted analysis separates F from three configurations only; between F, D and E the data cannot tell, which is a tie in the evidence, not a proof of equality.
misconceptions: Reads the highest point estimate as a shown ranking
Uses unadjusted tests after looking at fifteen pairs
Confuses not separated with shown to be equal

questions.prompt: A pilot of two configurations on 200 shared questions shows a 6-point difference and an SD of per-question differences of 0.25. The decision needs to detect 3 points. Which inputs should the sizing use?
options: The 6-point difference and SD 0.25
The 3-point minimum effect and SD 0.25
3 points and the SD of each configuration's scores
200 questions, since the pilot already found a difference
questions.explanation: The effect to detect comes from the decision, the noise from the pilot; the pilot's observed difference is itself uncertain and would undersize the study.
misconceptions: Sizes for the pilot's lucky draw instead of the effect that matters
Uses each score's spread, which ignores the pairing
Thinks the pilot's own n settles the question

questions.prompt: A new question costs SAR 15 and a sample with its grader call SAR 0.10. At temperature 0.8 within-item variance exceeds between-item variance. Which design is closest to the best at a fixed budget?
options: As many questions as possible, one sample each
Few questions, thirty samples each
Whatever K, since the grader cost does not enter
About ten to fifteen samples per question, the rest on questions
questions.explanation: K* = √((15 / 0.10) × within / between) is above 12 when within exceeds between; the optimum is flat around it.
misconceptions: Thinks only questions reduce variance, ignoring that sampling noise is the larger part here
Thinks cheap samples are always the answer, ignoring the between-item floor
Believes the cost of grading does not affect the choice

questions.prompt: D minus C is 2.2 points, paired and clustered 95% interval 0.5 to 3.9, minimum effect 3 points. Dr. Nadeen asks for one sentence. Which is right?
options: D is three points better; switch
D is better, but not shown to be better by three points
D is better, but by less than three points
No difference can be shown
questions.explanation: The interval excludes zero, so D is better; it includes values both below and above 3, so whether the gain reaches the minimum effect is not shown.
misconceptions: Reads significance as importance: the interval includes values below the threshold
Reads an interval that includes 3 as proof of an effect below 3
Uses the unpaired interval, which ignores that the questions are shared

questions.prompt: A new circular yields 25 questions; configuration D passes 24. The report needs a 95% interval for D's pass rate. Which choice is sound?
options: p ± 1.96 √(p(1 − p) / n), the standard formula
A bootstrap over the 25 questions
A Wilson or Jeffreys interval, or Clopper-Pearson if it supports a safety claim
No interval: 25 items are too few to say anything
questions.explanation: With few items near 1, Wald and the percentile bootstrap are too narrow; Wilson and Jeffreys keep close to 95%, Clopper-Pearson at least 95%.
misconceptions: Applies the large-sample formula where the lab showed it under-covers badly
Thinks a bootstrap fixes small samples; with 24 of 25 it inherits the same collapse
Believes small sets cannot be reported at all, when an honest wide interval is informative

questions.prompt: A configuration answers 60 safety questions with no unsafe answer. Which statement can the report make at 95% confidence?
options: Its unsafe rate on such questions is below about 5%
It never gives unsafe answers on such questions
Its unsafe rate is 0% ± 0
At most 3 of the next 60 answers will be unsafe
questions.explanation: With zero failures in n, the one-sided 95% upper bound on the failure rate is 1 − 0.051/n, about 3 / n: 4.9% for n = 60.
misconceptions: Turns zero observed failures into a claim of zero failures
Uses the Wald interval, which collapses to a point at 60 of 60
Confuses the bound for the rate with a bound on a count of future failures

questions.prompt: A grader agrees with people on 92% of 400 verdicts. In Arabic its specificity is 0.70; in English 0.92. What does that do to the pass rates it reports?
options: Nothing: 92% agreement is good enough
Arabic pass rates are understated
Both languages are biased equally, so comparisons are safe
Arabic pass rates are inflated more than English ones, shrinking any language gap
questions.explanation: Low specificity means bad answers are passed; more of them pass in Arabic, so Arabic rates rise more and a real Arabic weakness looks smaller.
misconceptions: Thinks high overall agreement makes the error rates irrelevant
Confuses specificity with sensitivity: low specificity passes bad answers, it does not fail good ones
Assumes errors in both directions cancel, which needs equal rates in both languages

questions.prompt: You corrected an Arabic pass rate with sensitivity and specificity from 150 labelled answers, and built the interval from the test set's clustered standard error only. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: the correction removes the grader's error
The interval ignores the uncertainty of sensitivity and specificity, so it is too narrow
The calibration set should have been clustered by document too
Corrected rates should be reported without intervals
questions.explanation: Sensitivity and specificity are estimates from a small labelled set; resampling it with the test set carries that uncertainty into the corrected rate's interval.
misconceptions: Thinks correction removes uncertainty instead of adding it
Confuses which set needs clustering: the calibration verdicts are separate answers
Believes a corrected rate cannot have an interval at all

questions.prompt: A grader's Arabic specificity is 0.73, from 49 human-failed answers. A team corrects an Arabic pass rate and reports an interval from the test set alone. What should the reviewer ask for?
options: Nothing: the corrected rate is unbiased
A Clopper-Pearson interval on the test set
An interval that also resamples the calibration verdicts
The uncorrected rate, which has a narrower interval
questions.explanation: Sensitivity and specificity are estimates from a small labelled set; their uncertainty belongs in the corrected rate's interval.
misconceptions: Thinks the correction makes the grader exact
Applies the small-set rule to the wrong quantity: the test set has hundreds of items
Removes the correction instead of measuring its uncertainty

questions.prompt: A report compares two configurations. One was scored as the best of five samples and tuned on 12 prompt variants using the test questions; the other as the mean of five, untuned. What must the audit do first?
options: Rescore both the same way and remove the test questions used in tuning before comparing
Add confidence intervals to the reported numbers
Ask for more test questions
Accept it: the tuned configuration earned its lead
questions.explanation: Unequal scoring and tuning on the test set are biases, not noise; only an equal-budget comparison on clean questions measures the configurations rather than the procedure.
misconceptions: Thinks an interval fixes a biased comparison; it only measures noise
Thinks a larger test set dilutes a bias that comes from how it was scored
Reads tuning on the test set as legitimate effort

questions.prompt: A report claims "the assistant is equally accurate for all regions". The logs carry no region field. How should the audit class the claim?
options: Supported: no regional difference was found
Unsupported: equal accuracy is unlikely
Supported, because regions should not matter for regulations
Untestable with these logs; name the data that would test it
questions.explanation: Without a region field no analysis of these logs can decide the claim; the memo says what data would.
misconceptions: Reads absence of evidence against the claim as evidence for it
Treats a claim the data cannot address as contradicted by them
Thinks a claim can be classed by the auditor's prior belief

questions.prompt: C's Arabic interval is 63.8 to 74.6 and its English interval 69.3 to 80.8. They overlap. Most documents have questions in both languages. What can you conclude about the gap?
options: No gap: the intervals overlap
Nothing yet: test the gap itself with a standard error clustered by document
Compute the gap's SE as the root sum of the two squared SEs
Report both rates; gaps are never tested
questions.explanation: Two slices that share documents are correlated; only an interval for the gap itself, clustered by document, says whether the gap is real.
misconceptions: Uses overlap as a test, which Day 2 showed ignores the shared structure
Treats the two slices as independent, when they share documents
Thinks slices are only descriptive and never tested

questions.prompt: A team's report has intervals, a plan and slices, but scores its own configuration as the best of five samples and the vendor's as the mean of five. Which field of the standard catches it?
options: multiplicity
slices
budget_parity, with the estimand stated per configuration
interval_method
questions.explanation: Budget parity requires every configuration to be scored and tuned the same way; a stated estimand makes the difference visible.
misconceptions: Multiplicity concerns how many comparisons, not how each was scored
Slices check groups of questions, not scoring rules
The interval method governs uncertainty, not the comparability of the scores

questions.prompt: An evaluation of a permits assistant reports 81% on 400 questions, 95% interval 77% to 85%. Which statement about the interval is correct?
options: It is a plausible range for the pass rate on new questions written the same way
It is the range of pass rates the assistant will reach next year
It is the range within which 95% of individual answers fall
It is the range of pass rates on these 400 questions if the evaluation were rerun with the same answers
questions.explanation: The interval estimates the pass rate on the population the questions were sampled from.
misconceptions: Extends the interval to a different population and time
Confuses an interval for a rate with a range of single outcomes
Treats the fixed sample as uncertain: on these questions with these answers the rate is known

questions.prompt: A configuration passes 270 of 300 independent questions. What is the formula standard error of its pass rate, to two significant figures?
misconceptions: Reports p(1 − p) without dividing by n or taking the root
Uses the number of failures as the standard error
Forgets the square root: 0.09 / 300 = 0.0003, then divides again

questions.prompt: A clustered standard error is 0.030 and the naive one is 0.020 on 900 questions. How many independent questions are the 900 worth?
misconceptions: Multiplies by the design effect instead of dividing
Uses the ratio of standard errors, 1.5, instead of its square
Multiplies by the ratio instead of dividing

questions.prompt: An evaluation set has 50 documents with 10 questions each and a design effect of 3. Which addition narrows the clustered interval most for the same 100 questions?
options: Five samples per question instead of one
Dropping the 10 documents with the most failures
Two more questions from each existing document
100 more questions from 10 new documents
questions.explanation: The clustered standard error falls with the number of independent clusters; new documents add them.
misconceptions: Confuses within-question sampling noise with between-document clustering
Removes data selectively, which biases the score
Treats extra questions from the same document as independent evidence

questions.prompt: At temperature 0.8 a configuration's within-item variance is 0.12 and its between-item variance 0.09. Going from 1 to 4 samples per question on 600 questions does what to the standard error?
options: Reduces it from about 0.0187 to about 0.0141
Reduces it to zero, because sampling noise disappears
Halves it, because four times the samples is like four times the questions
Leaves it unchanged, because samples of one question are not independent
misconceptions: Forgets the between-item part, which more samples do not reduce
Treats samples as if they were new questions
Thinks repeated samples add no information at all

questions.prompt: A permits assistant gives each applicant one answer. Which estimand should the release report use as its primary score?
options: The best of five samples chosen by the grader
The mean pass rate per sample
pass@5: right in at least one of five samples
pass^5: right in all five samples
questions.explanation: An applicant sees one answer, so the expected pass rate of a single sample is the quantity that matters.
misconceptions: Lets the grader choose after the fact, which no applicant can do
Describes a user who can retry and pick the right answer
Describes a stricter, consistency requirement rather than the single answer

questions.prompt: Two configurations are compared on four metrics, each tested at 5%. The report headlines whichever metric is significant. If the configurations are in fact identical, how often does such a report find a difference?
options: Exactly 20% of the time, four times 5%
About 5% of the time
More than 5%, up to about 19% if the metrics were independent
Never, because each test controls its own error
questions.explanation: Choosing the best of several tests after the results raises the chance of at least one false win; correlated metrics give a little less than 1 − 0.95⁴.
misconceptions: Adds the rates instead of combining them, and ignores correlation
Assumes the per-test error rate survives selection
Confuses per-test control with control of the whole study

questions.prompt: Which plan field, left empty, most directly allows the analyst to change the conclusion after seeing the results?
options: The owner's name
The list of secondary metrics
The date the evaluation ran
The decision rule linking each possible interval to an action
questions.explanation: Without a decision rule written in advance, any interval can be read as supporting the preferred action.
misconceptions: Names who is accountable but does not fix any analysis choice
Secondary results are labelled exploratory anyway
The run date is recorded by the logs and does not drive a conclusion

questions.prompt: Two configurations answer the same 600 questions; their per-question scores correlate at 0.8. Compared with an unpaired analysis, the paired standard error of their difference is:
options: Much smaller, because the shared question difficulty cancels
Zero, because the same questions were used
Larger, because pairing loses degrees of freedom
About the same, because the means are the same
questions.explanation: Var(D − C) = Var(D) + Var(C) − 2 Cov(C, D); a strong positive correlation removes most of the variance.
misconceptions: Thinks shared questions remove all noise, when per-question differences still vary
Overweights the loss of degrees of freedom, which is negligible with hundreds of questions
Confuses the point estimate, which is the same, with its precision

questions.prompt: The paired difference is 2.0 points, 95% interval 0.6 to 3.4, and the minimum effect is 3 points. Which verdict follows the plan?
options: Switch: the difference is significant
Better, but not shown to be better by the minimum effect
No difference shown
Worse than the minimum effect, so keep the old configuration as proven better
questions.explanation: The interval excludes zero but includes values below 3 points, so the gain is real but not shown to reach the threshold.
misconceptions: Treats statistical significance as practical importance
Ignores that the whole interval is above zero
Reads an interval that includes 3 as proof the effect is below 3

questions.prompt: Clustering by document widened each configuration's interval by half, but barely changed the paired interval of their difference. Why?
options: The paired analysis uses fewer questions
Clustering only applies to single scores by definition
The document effect moves both configurations together and cancels in the difference
The paired difference is always normally distributed
questions.explanation: A shared document effect raises or lowers both scores, so it drops out of D minus C.
misconceptions: Pairing uses the same questions, not fewer
Clustering applies to any statistic; it just may not matter
Normality has nothing to do with whether clustering matters

questions.prompt: Fifteen paired comparisons have smallest p-values 0.001, 0.004 and 0.006. Under Holm at 5%, which are separated?
options: The first two
All three
None
Only the first
questions.explanation: Holm compares 0.001 with 0.05/15 = 0.0033 (separated), then 0.004 with 0.05/14 = 0.0036 (fails) and stops.
misconceptions: Compares 0.004 with 0.05/13 or with 0.05 over its rank from the top, not with 0.05/14
Uses unadjusted 5% thresholds for every comparison
Thinks Bonferroni's threshold of 0.0033 rejects nothing, though 0.001 is below it

questions.prompt: A leaderboard of six configurations lists one rank per row. After Holm adjustment only the last configuration is separated from all others. What should the rank column show?
options: For each configuration, the range of ranks the data cannot rule out
Rank 1 for every configuration not separated from the leader
The point-estimate ranks, since adjustment applies only to p-values
Ranks rounded to the nearest pair
questions.explanation: Plausible rank ranges state what the adjusted comparisons support; single ranks claim separations that were not shown.
misconceptions: Treats not separated as tied for first, ignoring separations among the others
Thinks ranks are exempt from uncertainty
Invents a rounding with no statistical basis

questions.prompt: The SD of per-question paired differences is 0.20. How many shared questions detect a 4-point difference with 80% power at a two-sided 5% level, assuming independence?
options: About 98
About 196
About 1,960
About 50
misconceptions: Halves the answer by using one z value only
Forgets to square the effect in the denominator correctly
Uses the effect instead of its square

questions.prompt: A sizing formula gives 400 questions, but a simulation that resamples documents from the pilot shows 62% power at 400. What is the best reading?
options: The simulation is wrong because it is random
Use the formula; it is exact
An assumption of the formula fails for this data, probably clustering; size up and rerun the simulation
Lower the power target to 62%
questions.explanation: The simulation keeps the real cluster structure and the planned test; when it disagrees, the formula's assumptions are the suspect.
misconceptions: Mistakes Monte Carlo noise, which is small with enough draws, for bias
Trusts assumptions over the data's own structure
Changes the requirement to fit the plan

questions.prompt: A new question costs 100 times a sample, and the within-item variance equals the between-item variance. About how many samples per question minimise the variance at fixed cost?
options: As many as the budget allows
misconceptions: Uses the cost ratio without the square root
Ignores the between-item floor that samples cannot reduce
Spends everything on questions, ignoring sampling noise

questions.prompt: A 30-question set gives a pass rate of 29/30. Why is the normal-approximation interval a poor choice here?
options: Its estimated variance shrinks near 1, so it is too narrow and can pass 1
It assumes the questions are clustered
It cannot be computed for fewer than 50 items
It is too wide near 1
questions.explanation: Near 0 or 1 the plug-in variance p(1 − p)/n is small exactly where the estimate is least reliable, so coverage falls well below 95%.
misconceptions: Confuses the small-sample problem with clustering
Invents a hard limit; it can be computed but under-covers
Gets the direction of the error wrong

questions.prompt: In a simulation, an interval method covers the true rate in 87% of evaluations of 40 items at p = 0.95. What does that mean for a report that uses it?
options: Nothing, because coverage averages out over many reports
Its 95% intervals are, in effect, 87% intervals at such rates
It is 8 points more precise than claimed
The pass rates it reports are 8 points too high
questions.explanation: Coverage is the share of intervals that contain the truth; an 87% coverage means the stated 95% confidence is overstated.
misconceptions: Thinks under-coverage cancels across reports, when each report is overconfident
Reads under-coverage as extra precision
Confuses coverage of the interval with bias of the estimate

questions.prompt: A configuration passes all 100 questions of a safety set. What upper bound on its failure rate can be stated at 95% confidence?
options: About 1%
About 3%
About 5%
questions.explanation: With zero failures in n, 1 − 0.05^(1/n) ≈ 3/n = 3%.
misconceptions: Turns zero observed failures into a zero rate
Divides 1 by n instead of using the 95% bound
Uses 5 / n, mixing the level with the bound

questions.prompt: Two analysts report Beta posterior intervals for 40 out of 40: one with a uniform prior, one with a Jeffreys prior. Their lower ends differ by about 2.6 points. What should the report do?
options: Average the two intervals
Use whichever prior gives the higher lower end
Drop the Bayesian intervals because they disagree
State the prior used, and prefer the more cautious one for a safety claim
questions.explanation: At the edge the prior matters; stating it makes the claim checkable, and a safety claim should not lean on the more optimistic prior.
misconceptions: Averages two posteriors without any model that justifies it
Chooses the prior after seeing which looks better
Treats sensitivity to the prior as a reason to report nothing

questions.prompt: A model grader has specificity 0.70 in Arabic. What does that mean?
options: It passes 30% of answers that people fail
It agrees with people on 70% of Arabic verdicts
70% of the answers it passes are right
It fails 30% of answers that people pass
questions.explanation: Specificity is the share of truly failing answers the grader fails; the remaining 30% of failing answers are passed.
misconceptions: Confuses specificity with overall agreement
Describes the positive predictive value
Describes one minus sensitivity

questions.prompt: A grader's overall agreement with people is 91%. Its Arabic specificity is 0.73 and English 0.91. Which conclusion is right?
options: The grader is useless and must be replaced
Arabic pass rates are inflated more than English ones; correct them by language
Only English rates need correcting, since English agreement is higher
The grader is reliable; no correction is needed
questions.explanation: Agreement hides the class-specific errors; a lower Arabic specificity passes more bad Arabic answers.
misconceptions: Overreacts: a grader with known error rates can be corrected
Gets the direction wrong: the lower specificity is in Arabic
Trusts overall agreement, which is dominated by the common class

questions.prompt: The grader passes 70% of a configuration's answers; its sensitivity is 0.90 and specificity 0.80. What is the corrected pass rate?
options: About 78%
About 56%
About 71%
About 63%
misconceptions: Divides the observed rate by the sensitivity
Multiplies the observed rate by the specificity
Multiplies the observed rate by the sensitivity

questions.prompt: A corrected pass rate's interval was built from the test set's standard error alone. Its sensitivity and specificity came from 120 labelled answers. What does the interval miss?
options: The bias from the correction itself
Nothing, if the test set is large
The clustering of the calibration set by grader
The uncertainty in sensitivity and specificity, which a joint bootstrap or delta method adds
questions.explanation: Sensitivity and specificity are estimates; their sampling error passes into the corrected rate and must widen the interval.
misconceptions: The correction removes bias; the missing piece is variance
Thinks a large test set removes uncertainty in the calibration estimates
Invents a clustering that does not apply

questions.prompt: 48 test questions appear among the examples used to tune configuration D. On them D scores 90%; on the other questions 73%. Configurations A, B and C score the same on both groups. What follows?
options: D's lead comes partly from the overlap; compare on clean questions
D is better at hard questions
The overlap does not matter because it is under 10% of the set
The 48 questions are easier and should be dropped for every configuration
questions.explanation: The other configurations act as a control: the questions are not easier in general, so D's gain there comes from having seen them.
misconceptions: Reverses the evidence: the gain is on seen questions, not hard ones
Judges by the share of items, not by the size of the effect on the comparison
Ignores the control: A, B and C show the questions are not easier

questions.prompt: An overlap check by exact string match finds 8 Arabic test questions in the tuning examples; after folding hamza forms, ta marbuta, alef maqsura and diacritics it finds 21. Which count should the audit use?
options: The average, about 15
21, because spelling variants of the same question carry the same answer
Neither: Arabic overlap cannot be measured
8, because only identical strings are contamination
questions.explanation: A model that saw a question with a different hamza or diacritic has still seen the question; normalisation finds it.
misconceptions: Averages two measurements of which one is known to undercount
Gives up on a check that a simple normalisation makes reliable
Treats invisible spelling differences as different questions

questions.prompt: Configuration X is reported as pass@5 (best of five) and Y as the mean of five samples. X leads by 15 points. What is the fair comparison?
options: Compare X's best sample with Y's best sample on one question
Keep the reported numbers; both used five samples
Compare X's mean of five with Y's mean of five, or both at pass@5
Halve X's lead to correct for the extra samples
questions.explanation: The same estimand and budget for both; a different scoring rule is a different quantity.
misconceptions: Reduces the comparison to one question
Equal sample counts do not make different scoring rules comparable
Invents a correction factor with no basis

questions.prompt: A report claims a configuration 'will perform as well next year'. The authority has no data from next year's questions. How should the audit class it?
options: Supported, if the configuration ranks first
Supported, if this year's interval is narrow
Unsupported, because performance always drifts
Untestable with the data held; name the evaluation that would test it
questions.explanation: No data the authority holds come from that population, so the claim can be neither backed nor contradicted until a new evaluation exists.
misconceptions: Confuses a rank with a forecast
Extends this year's interval to another population
Asserts a contrary claim without data

questions.prompt: A claim says 'B is better than A'. The paired, clustered difference is 6.6 points, 95% interval 4.5 to 8.8. How should the audit class it?
options: Supported: the interval of the difference excludes zero
Unsupported: 6.6 points is small
Untestable: A and B are different models
Unsupported: the intervals of A and B overlap
questions.explanation: The claim is about direction, and the paired interval excludes zero; it is supported at the strength stated.
misconceptions: Imposes a size threshold the claim did not state
Thinks different systems cannot be compared
Uses overlap of separate intervals, which ignores the pairing

questions.prompt: Two language slices share 80 documents. Why is the standard error of the gap computed with document clustering rather than as √(SE_ar² + SE_en²)?
options: Because the Arabic slice is larger
Because a hard document lowers both languages, so the slices are correlated
Because clustering always gives a smaller standard error
Because the gap is a ratio, not a difference
questions.explanation: Shared documents make the two slice means correlated; the clustered contrast accounts for that, the independent formula does not.
misconceptions: Slice size affects each SE, not the method for the gap
Clustering can widen or narrow; it is about correctness, not size
The gap is a difference of rates

questions.prompt: After grader correction, C's Arabic minus English gap moves from −5.8 to −9.0 points, but its interval widens to −22.2 to +2.4. What should the report say?
options: There is no language gap, since the corrected interval includes zero
Report only the observed gap, which is significant
The best estimate of the gap is larger than observed; more Arabic labels are needed to pin it down
Average the observed and corrected gaps
questions.explanation: Correction removes the grader's bias and adds the calibration's uncertainty; both facts belong in the report, with the step that narrows the interval.
misconceptions: Reads a wide interval as evidence of no gap
Drops the correction because it is less convenient
Averages a biased and an unbiased estimate

questions.prompt: Which field of an evaluation reporting standard would have stopped a headline that compared one configuration's best of five samples with another's mean of five?
options: slices
interval_method
multiplicity
budget_parity, with the estimand stated per configuration
questions.explanation: Budget parity requires the same scoring and tuning for every configuration, and a stated estimand makes a mismatch visible.
misconceptions: Slices concern groups of questions
Interval method concerns uncertainty, not comparability
Multiplicity concerns the number of comparisons

questions.prompt: A team proposes making results by language optional in the reporting standard 'to keep reports short'. What is the strongest reason to keep them required?
options: An average can hide a configuration that serves one language worse, and graders can err unequally by language
Regulators ask for two numbers
Slices make every interval narrower
Arabic results are always lower
questions.explanation: Without slices a weakness in one language, possibly shrunk further by a lenient grader, never reaches the decision owner.
misconceptions: Appeals to a rule not stated in the course
Slices widen intervals; they are required for fairness, not precision
Asserts a fixed direction that the data did not show for every configuration
